title: How Many Giant-Killers Served David?
paragraphs:
How Many Giant-Killers Served David?
The Forgotten Warriors Behind the King—and What Their Story Reveals About the Jesus Who Rewrites Ours
Most people know the name Goliath.
Few remember the names of the men who kept killing giants after him.
That should make us pause.
Because sometimes the greatest miracle is not the victory everyone saw.
Sometimes the greater miracle is what that victory produced.

The Valley of Elah echoed with fear long before it echoed with faith. For forty days the armies of Israel listened to the taunts of a giant whose size seemed larger than their trust in God. Then a shepherd boy stepped forward carrying no sword, no armor, and no reputation worthy of military attention.
His confidence was not in himself.
His confidence was in the covenant God.

When David declared, “You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts” (1 Samuel 17:45), the Hebrew text preserves the divine name יהוה צְבָאוֹת (YHWH Tzeva’ot), “The LORD of Armies” or “The LORD of Hosts.”
David understood something Israel had forgotten.
The battle was never about the giant.
The battle was always about God.
The stone flew.
The giant fell.
History changed.
But that is not where the story ends.
In fact, that is where another story begins.
Years later, Scripture quietly reveals a remarkable truth that many believers overlook. David was not the only giant-killer in Israel.
He became the catalyst for an entire generation of giant-killers.

Second Samuel 21 and First Chronicles 20 record a series of battles against descendants of the Rephaim, a people known for extraordinary size and strength. These passages reveal at least four mighty warriors who struck down giants in addition to David's famous victory over Goliath.
There was Ishbi-benob, a giant whose spear weighed hundreds of shekels. David nearly lost his life against him until Abishai intervened and struck the giant down (2 Samuel 21:15-17).
There was Saph, another giant defeated by Sibbecai the Hushathite (2 Samuel 21:18).
There was Lahmi, the brother of Goliath, slain by Elhanan according to the clearer parallel account in 1 Chronicles 20:5.
There was the giant from Gath who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, defeated by Jonathan son of Shimei, David's relative (2 Samuel 21:20-21).
Then Scripture summarizes these victories with a statement that deserves more attention than it often receives:
“These four were descended from the giants in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants” (2 Samuel 21:22).
Notice the wording carefully.
Not only by the hand of David.
By the hand of his servants.
The shepherd who once stood alone had become a king surrounded by men who carried the same faith.
The boy who killed one giant inspired others to confront their own.
David's greatest achievement may not have been defeating Goliath.
It may have been raising giant-killers.
That truth reaches far beyond ancient battlefields.
Every believer faces giants.
Not necessarily nine-foot warriors wrapped in bronze armor.
But giants nonetheless.
Fear.
Addiction.
Shame.
Bitterness.
Depression.
Hidden sin.
Regret.
The crushing weight of failure.
Many people reading this know exactly what that feels like.
You smile in public.
You function at work.
You answer messages.
You attend church.
Yet deep inside, a giant keeps speaking.
“You'll never change.”
“You've gone too far.”
“God couldn't use someone like you.”
“You'll always be this way.”
The enemy has not changed his strategy.
He still speaks through fear.
He still magnifies impossibilities.
He still hopes God's people will believe the giant is bigger than God.
But the Gospel tells a different story.
The Gospel tells us that Jesus stepped onto a battlefield we could never win.
Where David faced Goliath, Christ faced sin, death, and hell itself.
Where David carried a stone, Jesus carried a cross.
Where David risked his life, Jesus willingly gave His.
Where David won a temporary victory, Christ secured an eternal one.
The Greek New Testament records Jesus' declaration from the cross:
Τετέλεσται (Tetelestai).
“It is finished” (John 19:30).
Not “I am finished.”
“It is finished.”
The debt was paid.
The victory was secured.
The work was accomplished.
The resurrection proved that death itself was not the final giant.
And because Christ conquered, He now transforms ordinary people into witnesses of extraordinary grace.
This is why our theme matters so deeply:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
David's story was not supposed to end with a throne.
Rahab's story was not supposed to end in the lineage of Christ.
Peter's story was not supposed to survive denial.
Paul's story was not supposed to emerge from persecution.
Your story may feel impossible right now.
But impossibility has never intimidated God.
The same Savior who rewrote theirs can rewrite yours.
Maybe your giant is a secret nobody knows.
Maybe your giant is a public failure everybody knows.
Maybe your giant is a wound that still bleeds years later.
Maybe your giant is your own reflection.
Yet Scripture repeatedly demonstrates that God specializes in taking broken people and turning them into living testimonies of His grace.
The Gospel is not self-improvement.
The Gospel is resurrection.
The Gospel is not behavior modification.
The Gospel is transformation.
The Gospel is not about making bad people slightly better.
It is about making spiritually dead people alive in Christ.
That is why the story of David's giant-killers matters.
The victory of one faithful servant inspired many others.
And that remains true today.
Every testimony gives someone else courage.
Every act of obedience strengthens another believer.
Every public declaration of faith encourages someone who feels alone.
Someone is watching how you endure suffering.
Someone is watching how you repent after failure.
Someone is watching how you trust Christ in uncertainty.
Someone is learning courage from your faithfulness.
Never underestimate what God can do through a surrendered life.
Perhaps the greatest tragedy in modern Christianity is not that believers face giants.
It is that many believers have forgotten Who stands with them.

The Aramaic expression often translated as “Son of Man,” בַּר אֱנָשׁ (Bar Enash), points us toward Jesus as both fully human and the promised Messiah. He entered our suffering, walked among us, carried our griefs, and defeated our greatest enemies.
He understands your battle.
He sees your wounds.
He knows your fears.
And He still calls you forward.
Not because you are strong.
Because He is.
Not because your faith is perfect.
Because His faithfulness is.
Not because you deserve grace.
Because grace is exactly what He came to give.
Maybe today you feel more like the frightened soldiers than David.
Good news.
The story is not over.
The God who raised giant-killers from shepherds still works in ordinary lives.
The Jesus who stepped out of the tomb is still rewriting stories.
The cross still saves.
The empty tomb still changes everything.
And grace still has the final word.
Someone needs this reminder today.

Not as a transaction, but as a partnership in spreading biblical truth, discipleship, encouragement, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ to more people around the world. If we truly desire to glorify God, supporting faithful Gospel-centered ministry and sharing Christ-centered content can become part of our worship and stewardship.
The giant was never the end of the story. It was only the introduction to what God could do through a life fully surrendered to Him.
